newsitem.title: GERMANY: Tax failure marks start of Kohl re-election bid.
newsitem.headline: Tax failure marks start of Kohl re-election bid.

text.p: By abandoning efforts to agree on a sweeping tax reform, German government and opposition leaders have effectively fired the starting gun for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's general election campaign.

The poll itself is more than a year away, but no one in Bonn doubts that the tax row will play a central role in Kohl's bid to claim a record sixth term in office and continue his drive for European political and economic integration.

Kohl's team are banking on being able to blame the opposition for the failure and for a general feeling of frustration among Germans that politicians are not doing enough to tackle major everyday problems such as massive unemployment.
The veteran chancellor had hoped to go into the campaign with a major package of popular tax cuts under his belt.
Opposition Social Democrat (SPD) leader Oskar Lafontaine was determined to block him, arguing the plans left gaping holes in the budget and were biased in favour of the rich.
Kohl himself drew up the battle lines at a news conference earlier this month, before he headed off on holiday. He pledged to take the tax reform issue to the voters in the September 1998 election.

"They know there is no alternative to our reform course. I am ready to make this argument a central theme of the election campaign. The coalition stands for modernisation and progress, the SPD embodies old thinking and immobility," he said.
Parliament's mediation committee was expected officially to throw out the tax reform plans on Wednesday, and was likely to approve only a tiny fraction of the proposals at most.

"Both sides are on a crash course. It's really no longer about solving the problem, about getting this tax reform, but about each side accusing the other of blame for the failure," RTL television political commentator Christoph Sagurna said.
"Of course, this is not how you get to solve problems a year before the general elections. At best, this is how you get into the Guinness Book of Records for the longest election campaign."
The business daily Handelsblatt believes Kohl's strategy could work.

"Lafontaine has made it his aim to let the coalition's tax reform suggestions fail completely," it said. "It's hardly to be expected that citizens, who are groaning under taxes which are too high in all classes, will reward him on polling day."
But the failure of the reform also contains dangers for Kohl's government.
The package thrown out on Wednesday contains plans to reduce the "solidarity surcharge" on income tax, originally imposed to help pay for the costs of German unification.

Kohl's junior coalition partners, the liberal Free Democrats, have made clear they want a special law to push through this measure on its own if the package as a whole fails. Some members have said the coalition's future hangs on the issue.

But Finance Minister Theo Waigel, needing every deutschemark he can get his hands on to ensure Germany makes the qualifying targets for Europe's planned single currency, has been noticeably reticent about whether he would sanction such a special bill.

Political analysts rate the chance that the coalition could collapse over the issue as slim. But it would produce a result which some commentators think would be preferable to a year of stagnation and party political games -- early elections.
"Let us vote as soon as possible!" pleaded Bonn's daily General-Anzeiger. "Maybe after that it will be possible to pursue fair and sensible policies again."
